'''''Felicia amoena''''', known as the '''soft felicia''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Soft Felicia - Encyclopedia of Life |url=https://eol.org/pages/6269609 |access-date=2025-05-19 |website=eol.org}}</ref> is a variably hairy, sometimes glandular, [[Biennial plant|biennial]] or [[perennial plant]], of about {{cvt|25|cm|frac=2}} high, that is assigned to the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is somewhat woody at its base, roots at the nodes if these contact the soil, and has ascending branches. The leaves are oppositely arranged along the stems at and just above a branching fork, further up the leaves alternate. The flower heads sit individually on up to {{cvt|12|cm|frac=2}} long stalks. They are {{cvt|2–3|cm|frac=5}} in diameter and consist of about twelve to twenty five heavenly blue ray florets that surround many yellow disc florets. Three subspecies have been recognised, that differ in width of the leaves and the involucral bracts, the size of the heads and number of ray florets and in having glandular hairs. These can be found in coastal sands and inland areas in the [[Western Cape]] and [[Eastern Cape]] provinces of South Africa.<ref name=Grau73>{{cite journal|first= J.|last= Grau|year= 1973|title= Revision der Gattung Felicia (Asteraceae)|journal= Mitteilungen der Botanischer Staatssammlung München|volume= IX|pages= 517–525|url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/15019162#page/533/mode/1up|access-date= 2017-11-12}}</ref> Flower heads can be found from June till October.<ref name=FNR>{{cite web|website= Fernkloof Nature Reserve|title= Felicia amoena subsp. amoena|url= http://www.fernkloof.org.za/index.php/all-plants/plant-families/item/felicia-amoena-subsp-amoena}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Felicia amoena'' subsp. ''amoena'' is an upright, up to {{cvt|25|cm|frac=2}} high, [[Biennial plant|biennial]], possibly sometimes [[Perennial plant|perennial]], sometimes near its base a bit woody herb, that mostly branches copiously. The branches are often crowded near the plants foot, while the [[Plant stem|node]]s that rest on the ground easily develop roots, the more distant parts of the side branches ascend. The [[Leaf#Arrangement on the stem|arrangement of the leaves on the stem]] changes from opposite to alternating. At the foot the leaves are in several opposite leaf pairs, and further upwards the leaves alternate, but after each branching, the lower one or two pairs are again opposite. The size of the leaves varies greatly, depending on the circumstances, and may be up to {{cvt|4|cm|frac=5}} long and 2{{frac|1|2}} mm (0.1 in) wide, linear to lance-shaped, bristly hairy, sometimes hairless with age, thick, with curled-down margins.<ref name=Grau73 />

The [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|flower heads]] sit individually on, up to {{cvt|12|cm|frac=2}} long, near the top densely felty hairy, [[Peduncle (botany)|stalks]], and emerge mostly with three together at the top of the branches. The [[Bract#Involucral bracts|involucre]] is up to {{cvt|7|mm}} in diameter and consists of a double row of bracts. The involucral bracts are line- to [[Glossary of leaf morphology#lanceolate|lance-shaped]], about {{cvt|5|mm|frac=5}} long and adorned with a brush-like tuft of hairs at their tips. The outer bracts are {{cvt|0.5|mm}} wide and carry arched bristles. The inner bracts are {{cvt|0.6|mm}} wide, slightly bristly and have a prominent midrib.

The [[Pseudanthium|flower heads]] have up to twenty five dark blue, female [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|ray florets]] with straps of about {{cvt|12|mm}} long and {{cvt|2|mm}} wide. These surround many [[Plant reproductive morphology#Terminology|bisexual]] disc florets with a yellow corolla up to {{cvt|3|mm}} long. In the center of each [[Petal#Corolla|corolla]] are five [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] merged into a tube, through which the [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] grows when the floret opens, hoovering up the [[pollen]] on its shaft. At the tip of both style branches is a triangular appendage. Surrounding the base of the corolla are many, white, serrated [[Pappus (botany)|pappus bristles]] of about {{cvt|3|mm}} long. The eventually dark brown, dry, one-seeded, [[Dehiscence (botany)|indehiscent]] fruits called [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|cypselae]] are inverted egg-shaped, about {{cvt|2.5|mm}} long and {{cvt|1.2|mm}} wide, with a prominent ridge along the margin, with some scales on its surface and short, forked hairs.<ref name=Grau73 />

''Felicia amoena'' subsp. ''latifolia'' is a [[Ploidy#Diploid|diploid]] having eight sets of homologue chromosomes (2n=16).<ref name=Grau73 />

=== Differences between the subspecies ===
''Felicia amoena'' and its three subspecies are among the most variable [[taxon|taxa]] in the [[genus]]. Subsp. ''amoena'' is mostly a biennial, has linear to lance-shaped leaves of up to {{cvt|4|cm|frac=5}} long and 2{{frac|1|2}} mm (0.1 in) wide, with a blunt or slightly pointy tip. Its involucres are relatively large, about {{cvt|7|mm}} in diameter and bracts of about {{cvt|5|mm}} long and {{cvt|0.5–0.6|mm}} wide. It has up to twenty five ray florets of about 12 mm long and 2 mm wide surrounding yellow disc florets. Subsp. ''latifolia'' has broader leaves, that are lance-shaped to inverted egg-shaped, 4–1{{frac|3|4}} cm long and 4{{frac|1|2}}–10 mm wide. It also has wider involucral bracts at about 5{{frac|1|2}} mm long and {{cvt|0.9–1.2|mm}} wide. The disc florets often turn dark red with age. Subsp. ''stricta'' is always a perennial with a woody base, slightly sticky because it has glandular hairs, and has small and narrow, pointy leaves of 1–1{{frac|3|4}} cm long and {{cvt|2–4|mm}} wide, almost all of which are opposite. Its involucres are relatively small, about {{cvt|5|mm}} in diameter, with bracts only {{cvt|4|mm}} long, with only about twelve ray florets of 8 mm long and 1{{frac|1|2}} mm wide.<ref name=Grau73 />

== Taxonomy and naming ==
As far as known, the first specimen of this daisy species was [[Plant collecting|collected]] in 1826, where the road from the Potberg crosses the [[Breede River]], by Cape Town organ player [[Baron von Ludwig#Business interests|Ludwig Beil]]. It is now assigned to the subspecies ''latifolia''. A plant collected by [[Johann Franz Drège]] at [[Riebeek-Kasteel]], was described by [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in 1836, who called it ''Agathaea stricta'', is now assigned to subsp. ''stricta''. The first specimen now assigned to subspecies ''amoena'' was collected from [[Hout Bay]] on the west coast of the Cape Peninsula by [[Christian Ferdinand Friedrich Krauss]] in 1838. It was described in 1843 by [[Carl Heinrich "Bipontinus" Schultz]], who named it ''Agathaea amoena''. In 1865, [[William Henry Harvey]], who was a [[Lumpers and splitters|lumper]], sunk ''Agataea'' in ''Aster'', creating the combination ''Aster amoenus''. He distinguished a slightly different specimen, that had been collected by [[Karl Wilhelm Ludwig Pappe]], and named it after him ''Aster pappei''. Harvey further distinguished ''Aster elongatus'' var. ''spathulaefolius'' in the same publication. Finally Harvey regarded De Candolle's specimen as a variety that should be placed under [[Christian Friedrich Lessing]]'s species ''Aster adfinis'' (now ''[[Felicia dubia]]''), creating the combination ''Aster adfinis'' var. ''stricta''. In 1948, the eminent South African botanist [[Margaret Levyns]] created the combination ''Felicia amoena'', that is still in use today. In his 1973 ''[[Taxonomy (biology)#Monograph and taxonomic revision|Revision]] of the genus Felicia (Asteraceae)'', [[Jürke Grau]] distinguished three subspecies: ''F. amoena'' subsp. ''amoena'', ''F. amoena'' subsp. ''stricta'', and his new taxon ''F. amoena'' subsp. ''latifolia''.  The species is considered to be part of the [[Section (botany)|section]] [[Felicia (plant)#Neodetris|Neodetris]].<ref name=Grau73 />

The species [[epithet]] ''amoena'' means "beautiful" or "pleasing" and is said to refer to the attractive flower heads.<ref name=FNR />

== Distribution, habitat and ecology ==
''Felicia amoena'' subsp. ''amoena'' has the smaller distribution of the three subspecies. It is restricted to the sandy soils around the [[Cape Peninsula]] and near Gordons Bay. Subsp. ''latifolia'' has the largest area and occurs along the coast from the Cape Peninsula in the very west to the mouth of the [[Sundays River]] in the east. An isolated population also occurs in the southern Cedarberg. Subsp. ''stricta'' can be found inland, from the Cedarberg in the north, via the [[Piketberg]] along the western edge, around [[Ceres, Western Cape|Ceres]], near [[Worcester, Western Cape|Worcester]] and [[Swellendam]] on the eastern edge to [[Bredasdorp]] in the south.<ref name=Grau73 />

== Conservation ==
The continued survival of all three subspecies of ''Felicia amoena'' is considered to be of [[Least-concern species|least concern]] because their populations are stable.<ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Felicia amoena subsp. amoena|url= http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3052-7}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Felicia amoena subsp. latifolia|url= http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3052-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website= SANBI Red List of South African Plants|title= Felicia amoena subsp. stricta|url= http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3052-9}}</ref>
